chunks: "Ground bounce is the voltage that appears on a chip's internal ground, relative to the board ground, when a lot of current changes quickly through the ground pin or bond wire.
That path has inductance, maybe a couple of nanohenries, so the voltage is V equals L di over dt .

If eight outputs switch high-to-low at once, all their discharge current flows back through the same package ground inductance, the di/dt adds up, and the chip's ground node lifts by hundreds of millivolts for a nanosecond or so.

What you see is the chip's quiet outputs that are supposed to stay low jumping up with the bounce, which can false-trigger the next chip, and the chip's own inputs seeing their thresholds shifted because their reference moved.
You can get double clocking, resets, or corrupted data that only happens when a wide bus changes.

To reduce it, I cut L or di over dt : more ground pins in parallel, a package with shorter leads like a BGA, slower edges using slew-rate control or series resistors, fewer outputs switching at the same moment, and good decoupling and a solid ground plane right at the part."
